title: Deadbot
summary:
A deadbot, deathbot, or griefbot is a digital avatar created with artificial intelligence which resembles a person who is dead. Griefbots employ natural language processing and machine-learning techniques to approximate the style and personality of a deceased person. Deadbots are chatbots that imitate the personality, linguistic style, and even the voice and virtual avatar of a deceased individual by being trained on the digital legacy they left behind, such as chat logs, emails, social media posts, and voice recordings.

This burgeoning industry has its origins in programmer Jason Rohrer's Project December, a deadbot generator developed in 2019 with GPT-3 beta software provided by OpenAI. One of the earliest users, Canadian Joshua Barbeau, documented an encounter with his dead girlfriend, Jessica. In January 2021, Microsoft was granted a patent for such an individualized chatbot system.

Cultural acceptance varies: while some view deadbots as expressions of remembrance, others regard them as unsettling or ethically problematic. Key ethical issues include consent, as development or use must correspond to what the imitated person agreed to; manipulation risks, with research highlighting the potential for companies to use deadbots to surreptitiously advertise products in the manner of a departed loved one or distress children by insisting a dead parent is still with them; and emotional vulnerability, as people might develop strong emotional bonds with such simulations, making them particularly vulnerable to manipulation.

The digital afterlife industry may reach near $80 billion in a decade, fueled by AI deadbots. Recommendations for safeguards include developing sensitive procedures for retiring deadbots, ensuring meaningful transparency through disclaimers on risks and capabilities, restricting access to adult users only, and following the principle of mutual consent of both data donors and recipients.
